sources.title: Dash Academy curriculum, module 3 (What is Dash Platform?)
State Transition (incl. shielded types and credit rate)
Dash Platform Book CHANGELOG (shielded pool rollout)

claims.text: Dash Platform is a decentralized data-storage and application layer on top of Dash; Dash Core is the layer-1 payment layer. Platform stores structured state governed by schemas and signed state transitions rather than running arbitrary user-written code.
Drive is Platform's storage component, hosted by the masternode (evonode) network, and holds current Platform state; each registered data contract has its own application state within it.
A document is an application record associated with a data contract, carrying application fields plus base fields such as identifier, document type, revision, contract id, and owning identity.

A data contract is the schema that declares the document types an application may store and the fields and indexes those records satisfy; a write succeeds only if the resulting data matches the schema.
An identity is a persistent Platform account with public keys and a credit balance that owns data and authorizes changes through signed state transitions.
DPNS registers human-readable names and associates them with identities; it is implemented as an application on top of Platform and is a capability Dash Core alone does not provide.
DAPI is a decentralized HTTP/gRPC API served by masternodes that exposes both Core and Platform over one interface; SDKs wrap it and let clients connect without running their own node.
Queries can return locally verifiable cryptographic proofs (inclusion and non-inclusion) so a client can verify a response against committed state instead of trusting the node that answered.

Configurable application tokens are first-class protocol objects declared in a data contract (like ERC-20 style assets) with built-in mint, transfer, burn, freeze, and a direct-purchase action paid in credits.
An NFT is not a separate standard: it is a uniquely identified Platform document with built-in transfer and a set-price purchase mechanism handled by the protocol.

The shielded pool moves value privately via Orchard/Halo2 zero-knowledge proofs (shield, shielded transfer, unshield, shielded withdrawal); pool types are credit pool (0), main token pool (1), and individual token pool (2).
Shielding privatizes movement of value; it does not make application documents private. Documents remain replicated, queryable state.

Shielded-pool availability is version-dependent: Docs 3.1.0 lists the shielded endpoints as added in 3.1.0 but 'not yet available on public nodes', while the v4.2-dev book documents pool seeding at genesis and gating behind protocol v12.
Credits pay for Platform work (storage and processing fees). They are established by locking Dash on Core; state transition fees are charged against an identity's credit balance.
Platform addresses are bech32m (DIP-18) destinations that can hold Platform credits and fund identity operations without a pre-existing identity.
Because anyone can top up any identity's credit balance, an application can sponsor its users' fees by paying for their operations.

An app's frontend and custom business logic run where the developer chooses; the network's responsibility is keeping the shared records, their ownership, and the rules that validate changes. Third-party fee funding is a client-side convention, not a protocol requirement.

conflicts.topic: Shielded pool public-network availability is contested between Dash Platform Docs 3.1.0 and the v4.2-dev Platform Book
conflicts.resolution: Describe the pool's purpose (private movement of value via zero-knowledge proofs) and its privacy boundary (application documents stay public) at concept level. Omit any mainnet-availability date, and do not repeat module 4's 'not yet available on public nodes' sentence verbatim. The version conflict is recorded here rather than resolved into a forward-looking claim.

uncertainties.topic: How much of the token-vs-NFT transfer/purchase mechanics belongs in this overview
uncertainties.resolution: Name the distinction (interchangeable configured token vs unique transferable document) and that transfer and set-price purchase are protocol features, without enumerating the token action set or pricing. The action inventory belongs to later modules.

uncertainties.topic: Whether the lesson should make a forward-looking statement about shielded-pool availability
uncertainties.resolution: Describe purpose and privacy boundary only; omit any availability date (see conflict V1).

uncertainties.topic: The committed what-is-dash-platform.mdx and its evidence ledger predate the expanded manifest
uncertainties.resolution: Re-author the lesson around the current manifest rather than patching the stale draft. The through-line (record after payment -> valid record needs an author -> pick the layer) is kept, with DAPI/proofs, tokens/NFTs, the shielded pool, credits/addresses/sponsorship, and the assembled example added.

priorKnowledge: What a blockchain is: an append-only ledger with hash-linked blocks, signatures, consensus, and expense-to-rewrite (content/academy/what-is-a-blockchain.mdx, 'A log that grows at one end', 'What makes rewriting expensive').

Dash Core as the payment layer: InstantSend locks inputs before a block, ChainLocks protect the block, and masternodes are the collateralized second tier that supplies these services (content/academy/what-is-dash.mdx, 'Who makes the lock stick?', 'Why the checkout benefits from both').

The one-line handoff to Platform at the end of the prerequisite: 'Dash also supports applications beyond payments through Dash Platform, an application-data layer hosted by a type of masternode called an Evolution masternode' (content/academy/what-is-dash.mdx, final paragraph).

Glossary terms already defined and reusable via <Term>: masternode, evonode, state-transition, dpns, dapi, drive, data-contract, identity, smart-contract, dapp, state-proof, light-client, grovedb, duff (lib/glossary.ts).
teachingPlan.centralQuestion: I've settled a Dash payment, but my app still needs its own records — usernames, orders, status. Where does that data live once it isn't in my own database, and what can I build on top of it?
teachingPlan.likelyMistake: Treating Platform either as a private database (assuming data sent there is confidential) or as a general-purpose smart-contract chain, and consequently misrouting features: putting payment-only features on Platform, or expecting arbitrary uploaded code and on-network secrets to be possible there.
teachingPlan.workedExample: A small invented app: an event organizer (Ada) sells limited-edition seat passes. Core settles the Dash payment; a DPNS name brands the festival; each seat pass is a unique transferable document under Ada's data contract, bought at a set price using the protocol's built-in purchase; buyer identities own their passes; the network stores and validates the records in Drive while the app tops up buyers' credit balances, and the ticket-sales frontend plus pricing logic stay on Ada's own servers. The example shows several features cooperating and marks the boundary between Ada's code and the network's work.
reasoningChain: Accepting a Dash payment still leaves the app needing records a payment can't carry, which raises where shared application data lives without a private database.
A shared store is only useful if what may be stored is agreed, so a data contract states the rules and documents are the records that satisfy them, held in Drive.
A valid record still needs an author, so identities own data and sign the changes, and DPNS attaches readable names to those identities.
An app can't practically reach shared state by running its own node, so DAPI and the SDKs connect clients, which raises how to trust an answering server.
Query proofs resolve that: a client verifies a response against committed state instead of trusting the node that answered.

Knowing the store holds more than plain rows, ask what kinds of asset those records can be: interchangeable value is a configured token, a specific ownable thing is a unique transferable document (NFT), both with transfer and purchase built in.
Putting records on a shared network raises what stays private: the shielded pool moves value privately, but documents themselves remain public state.
All that network work has a metering cost: credits (from Dash locked into a Platform address) pay it, and because anyone can top up an identity, an app can sponsor its users' fees.
The closing example assembles several of these pieces into one app and makes explicit which responsibilities are the developer's and which are the network's.
continuityGaps: The prerequisite's handoff names an 'Evolution masternode', but the glossary term is 'evonode'; the lesson lands on 'evonode' rather than propagating 'Evolution masternode'.

Credits, DAPI, SDKs, and the shielded pool are first introduced here, but several are already glossary-defined, so reuse <Term> rather than re-defining inline where the sentence does not depend on the meaning.

The committed why-build-on-dash.mdx (module 4) asserts the shielded-pool endpoints are 'not yet available on public nodes', which may itself be stale; module 3 must not repeat that availability claim verbatim (uncertainty U2 / conflict V1).

No prior lesson defines what a Platform identity's keys are for (purposes/security levels are mustNotCover here), so the lesson describes ownership and authorization at effect level without touching key derivation.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can describe Platform as an application layer on Dash, distinguish it from Core payments, and recognise a feature that needs Platform
coverageMap.demonstration: A checkout that only moves Dash routes to Core; a shared profile its owner edits, or a readable name, routes to Platform, and one shop can use both at once.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can describe identities as accounts that own data and authorize actions, and Dash names (DPNS) as readable names associated with identities
coverageMap.explanation: A valid record still needs an author
coverageMap.demonstration: A user's profile and readable name both belong to the user's identity, which signs authorized changes to what it owns; another identity's well-formed replacement is refused.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can describe Drive as shared network storage, documents as application records, and data contracts as the rules for those records
coverageMap.demonstration: A profile is a document held in Drive; a data contract declares the fields and rules the profile must satisfy before a write is accepted.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can say how DAPI and SDKs connect an app to Platform, and what verifiable queries offer beyond trusting a responding server
coverageMap.demonstration: The app talks through DAPI and the SDKs without running a node, and a state proof ties a query answer to committed state so the client verifies it rather than trusting the replying node.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can distinguish configurable application tokens from unique transferable records or NFTs, including built-in transfer and purchase capabilities
coverageMap.demonstration: A loyalty currency is a configured token with any two units interchangeable; a numbered seat is a unique NFT document, with transfer and set-price purchase built into the protocol.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can describe shielded Dash or shielded balances as private movement of value through Platform's shielded pool, without assuming application documents become private
coverageMap.demonstration: The shielded pool conceals value movement's sender, receiver, and amount, while documents in Drive remain replicated, queryable state.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can recognise credits as payment for Platform work, Platform addresses as funding destinations, and fee sponsorship as something an app can provide
coverageMap.demonstration: An empty-account buyer is topped up by Ada; credits (created by locking Dash, held at a Platform address) pay the network work, so sponsorship is just an app funding someone's balance.

coverageMap.requirement: the learner can connect several Platform features in one small application example and distinguish the app's frontend and custom logic from the network's responsibilities
coverageMap.demonstration: Ada's festival app holds passes in Drive, sells them at a set price as NFTs, brands the sale with a DPNS name, and sponsors buyers' credits; the ticket page and pricing run on Ada's servers while the network keeps ownership and rules.
